title: What Is RSO? Rick Simpson Oil and What Research Says
h1: Rick Simpson Oil: Its Story, How It's Made and What Research Says
metaDescription: What is RSO? An honest guide to Rick Simpson oil: its story, how it differs from CBD oil, how it's made and taken, side effects, and what research shows.

body:
What is RSO? RSO, short for Rick Simpson oil, is a thick, dark cannabis extract made from the whole flower of THC-rich plants. Instead of isolating one compound, it keeps most of what the flower contains, so it is potent and strongly intoxicating. RSO became famous through bold cancer claims, and those claims rest on personal stories, not clinical trials. Here's what it is, how it's made and taken, and what research does and doesn't show.

## What is RSO? A full-extract, high-THC oil

RSO belongs to a family of products called full-extract cannabis oil, or FECO, and some shoppers simply call it RSO oil. Makers soak cannabis flower in a solvent, strain out the plant material and remove the solvent, leaving a sticky, tar-like oil. The name describes a style of extract, not a brand.

Because it starts with THC-dominant flower, RSO packs a lot of THC into a little oil. It usually comes in a syringe, since it's too thick to pour, so the milligram count on the label is the number to read first. Our [guide to shopping for RSO](/blog/shopping-for-rso-guide/) walks through syringe labels and testing details.

## Rick Simpson's story and the claims around it

The oil is named for Rick Simpson, a Canadian medical cannabis activist best known for popularizing cannabis oil as a home remedy for skin cancer. In 2003, he claimed that a high-THC oil he extracted himself cured his basal cell carcinoma, a common type of skin cancer. Retellings of the story differ on the details, and the claim rests on his own account, but it spread widely online, including through a documentary about him.

One account, however moving, can't show cause and effect. A single story leaves other explanations for what happened wide open. That's why researchers rely on controlled trials, and why RSO has never been approved as a cancer treatment.

## Cannabinoids and cancer: what lab studies show

Lab research gives the cancer claims their scientific gloss. In cell and animal studies reviewed by the National Cancer Institute, cannabinoids killed some tumor cells while sparing normal ones, and some animal studies showed tumors shrinking. Those are early findings, and plenty of compounds that look promising in a dish never work in people.

Human evidence is where the story falls apart. The National Cancer Institute notes that highly concentrated THC and CBD oils are illegally promoted as potential cancer cures, even though they have never been evaluated in clinical trials for anticancer activity or safety. A 2022 review of 77 published case reports judged most of them too weak to support an anticancer effect and found no strong clinical trial data behind the lab results. The FDA has not approved cannabis or cannabinoids as a cancer treatment.

The bottom line: RSO has never been tested against cancer in a clinical trial, and there is no trial evidence that it shrinks tumors or works against cancer in people. Don't swap or delay cancer care for it.

## Where the evidence is stronger: approved cannabinoid medicines

Some cannabinoid medicines do have solid backing for specific uses. The FDA has approved dronabinol, a synthetic form of THC, for nausea caused by cancer chemotherapy and for appetite loss tied to weight loss in people with AIDS. It has also approved nabilone, a lab-made compound similar to THC, for chemotherapy nausea.

These are pharmacy medicines with measured doses, tested in clinical trials. RSO isn't one of them, and the FDA has not approved cannabis itself for any disease or condition. If nausea or appetite is a struggle during cancer care, ask your oncology team about the options that have been studied.

## RSO vs CBD oil: how they differ

| | RSO | Typical CBD oil |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Starting plant | THC-dominant cannabis flower | Usually hemp |
| Main cannabinoid | THC | CBD |
| Intoxicating? | Yes, strongly | Not the way THC is |
| Texture | Thick, sticky paste | Thin oil, often mixed with a carrier oil |
| Usual package | Syringe | Dropper bottle |

Some products blend the two, such as RSO made with a set ratio of THC to CBD, so check the milligrams of each on the label.

## How licensed processors make RSO

Licensed processors follow the same basic idea at a larger scale: soak, strain, then remove the solvent. Ethanol is a common choice, and it is evaporated off to leave the concentrated oil. Extraction solvents like ethanol are flammable, a big reason extraction belongs in licensed facilities rather than home kitchens.

Every product on our shelves comes from trusted vendors and has passed Michigan testing. For a wider look at the process, see our [overview of cannabis extraction methods](/blog/types-of-cannabis-extraction/).

## How to use RSO: common ways people take it

Most people take RSO by mouth:

- **On or under the tongue:** a very small amount squeezed from the syringe.
- **In food:** stirred into a spoonful of something, like peanut butter.
- **In capsules:** some products come pre-measured.
- **On skin:** some people apply it topically, though topical use hasn't been well studied.

RSO isn't made for smoking. Swallowed THC is absorbed slowly and processed by the liver, which turns some of it into another potent compound, so it takes longer to kick in than inhaled cannabis and lasts longer, too. Our guide to [how THC works in the body](/blog/what-is-thc-benefits-effects/) explains why.

## RSO side effects, and starting small

Because RSO is concentrated THC, its effects can be strong. The National Cancer Institute lists possible cannabis side effects including a fast heartbeat, low blood pressure, dizziness, drowsiness and, for some people, paranoia or hallucinations. Concentrated cannabinoids can also interact with medicines: the institute notes that CBD may block liver enzymes that process many drugs, including some cancer therapies.

There's no standard RSO dosage, and syringes vary widely in strength. If you and your doctor decide it's worth trying:

1. Start with the smallest amount you can measure.
2. Wait before taking more, because swallowed THC builds slowly.
3. Don't drive or operate machinery after using it.
4. Store syringes locked up, out of reach of children and pets.

RSO is for adults 21+, or patients 18+ with a Michigan medical card. Please consume responsibly.

## Talking to your doctor, and Michigan's medical program

Talk with your doctor before using RSO, and with your oncologist if you're in cancer care. That matters even more if you're pregnant or breastfeeding, take other medicines, or have heart, liver or mental health conditions.

Michigan's medical marijuana program lists cancer among its qualifying conditions. A medical card is a legal status, though, not a sign that cannabis will help a particular condition. Our pages on [getting a Michigan medical card](/getting-a-medical-card/) and the [patient guide](/patient-guide/) explain the process.

Registered patients 18 and older with a valid card are welcome at High Society. If you have a question about a product label, [find your nearest store](/dispensary-locations/) and ask our team in person.

faq.a: There's no reliable evidence that it can. Lab and animal studies have found that some cannabinoids affect cancer cells, but no strong clinical trial evidence shows that RSO or any cannabis oil works against cancer in people, and the FDA hasn't approved cannabis as a cancer treatment. If you're considering RSO during cancer care, talk with your oncologist first, partly because concentrated cannabinoids can interact with some cancer drugs.

faq.q: Is RSO the same as CBD oil?
faq.a: No. RSO is made from THC-rich cannabis flower and is strongly intoxicating, while most CBD oils come from hemp and contain mostly CBD with little THC. RSO is a thick paste sold in a syringe; CBD oil is usually a thin oil in a dropper bottle. Some RSO-style products blend THC and CBD, so check the label for the milligrams of each.

faq.q: What are common ways to take RSO?
faq.a: Most people take it by mouth: a very small amount on or under the tongue, stirred into food, or in a pre-measured capsule. Some apply it to the skin, though topical use hasn't been well studied. Because swallowed THC builds slowly and lasts for hours, start with the smallest amount you can measure and wait before taking more.

faq.q: What side effects can RSO cause?
faq.a: RSO is concentrated THC, so effects can be strong. Possible cannabis side effects include a fast heartbeat, dizziness, drowsiness, low blood pressure and, for some people, paranoia or hallucinations. Concentrated cannabinoids may also interact with medicines, including some cancer drugs. Talk with your doctor before trying it, and get medical help right away if you feel severely unwell.

claims.claim: RSO is a thick, high-THC full-extract cannabis oil (FECO): flower soaked in a solvent, strained, solvent removed; the name is a style of extract, not a brand
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10501512/ (Mamo 2021: "high-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) oil"); WebMD RSO overview, reviewed 2026-07-14 ("highly concentrated, full-extract cannabis oil (FECO)"; solvent "boiled off"); Viviers 2022 J Cannabis Res ("Rick Simpson oils" or "FECO's")

claims.claim: RSO usually comes in a (plastic) syringe because it is too thick to pour
claims.source: WebMD RSO overview ("commonly sold in a syringe because it's a thick, sticky oil")

claims.claim: Rick Simpson, a Canadian engineer turned activist, said that in 2003, after a doctor removed a basal cell skin cancer, he put homemade oil on his bandages and the cancer cleared within days
claims.fix: Retellings disagree (WebMD: oil on bandages after the removal; other accounts: oil on other, untested spots), and the peer-reviewed source gives only the core. Rewritten to: Canadian medical cannabis activist best known for popularizing cannabis oil for skin cancer; claimed in 2003 that his own high-THC oil cured his basal cell carcinoma; details differ and rest on his own account; the story spread online, including a documentary.
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10501512/ ("Cannabis oil as a homeopathic remedy for skin cancer was most popularized by Rick Simpson, a Canadian medical marijuana activist"; "In 2003, Rick Simpson claimed that he was able to cure his basal cell carcinoma"; online documentary)

claims.claim: He spent years sharing his recipe online
claims.fix: Removed; WebMD says only that his website explains how to make the oil.
claims.source: WebMD RSO overview ("On his website, Simpson doesn't sell the oil, but he does explain how to make it")

claims.claim: His original method used naphtha, a flammable petroleum solvent
claims.fix: Removed with the WebMD citation (replaced by a peer-reviewed source); the processing section now says extraction solvents like ethanol are flammable.
claims.source: WebMD RSO overview ("soaking whole cannabis plants in naphtha")

claims.claim: No health agency has backed RSO as a cancer remedy
claims.fix: Universal claim narrowed to what the sources state: RSO has never been approved as a cancer treatment.
claims.source: https://www.cancer.gov/about-cancer/treatment/cam/patient/cannabis-pdq ("The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has not approved Cannabis or cannabinoids for use as a cancer treatment.")

claims.claim: In cell and animal studies reviewed by NCI, cannabinoids killed some tumor cells while sparing normal ones; some animal studies showed tumors shrinking
claims.source: https://www.cancer.gov/about-cancer/treatment/cam/hp/cannabis-pdq ("Cannabinoids appear to kill tumor cells but do not affect their nontransformed counterparts"; "induce regression of glioma tumors in mice and rats")

claims.claim: NCI: highly concentrated THC and CBD oils are illegally promoted as potential cancer cures and have never been evaluated in clinical trials for anticancer activity or safety
claims.source: https://www.cancer.gov/about-cancer/treatment/cam/hp/cannabis-pdq ("Highly concentrated THC or cannabidiol (CBD) oil extracts are illegally promoted as potential cancer cures." "These oils have not been evaluated in any clinical trials for anticancer activity or safety.")

claims.claim: A 2022 review of 77 case reports judged most too weak to support an anticancer effect and found no strong clinical trial data
claims.source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34370591/ (abstract via NCBI E-utilities: 77 case reports; 81% weak; "No strong clinical trial data exist to confirm the pre-clinical studies"; Cannabis Cannabinoid Res 2022;7(1):24-33)

claims.claim: The FDA has not approved cannabis or cannabinoids as a cancer treatment
claims.source: https://www.cancer.gov/about-cancer/treatment/cam/patient/cannabis-pdq (verbatim)

claims.claim: There is no clinical evidence that RSO shrinks tumors or works against cancer in people
claims.fix: Weak case reports are clinical evidence of a kind; now: RSO has never been tested against cancer in a clinical trial, and there is no trial evidence that it works.
claims.source: https://www.cancer.gov/about-cancer/treatment/cam/hp/cannabis-pdq (oils "have not been evaluated in any clinical trials for anticancer activity or safety")

claims.claim: No clinical trial has shown that RSO or any cannabis oil works against cancer (takeaway, FAQ)
claims.fix: The 2022 review notes two small glioblastoma trials reporting survival data; now: no strong clinical trial evidence shows that RSO or any cannabis oil works against cancer.
claims.source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34370591/ ("No strong clinical trial data exist to confirm the pre-clinical studies")

claims.claim: FDA approved dronabinol (synthetic THC) for chemotherapy nausea and vomiting and for appetite loss with weight loss in AIDS; nabilone (lab-made cannabinoid) for chemotherapy nausea
claims.fix: Wording aligned to the cited FDA page: "nausea caused by cancer chemotherapy"; nabilone "a lab-made compound similar to THC".
claims.source: https://www.fda.gov/news-events/public-health-focus/fda-and-cannabis-research-and-drug-approval-process (dronabinol "for nausea associated with cancer chemotherapy" and "anorexia associated with weight loss in AIDS patients"; nabilone "has a chemical structure similar to THC and is synthetically derived")

claims.claim: The FDA has not approved any cannabis plant product for a disease or condition
claims.fix: The FDA approved Epidiolex, a cannabis-derived drug; now: the FDA has not approved cannabis itself to treat any disease or condition.
claims.source: https://www.fda.gov/news-events/public-health-focus/fda-and-cannabis-research-and-drug-approval-process ("the FDA has not approved a marketing application for cannabis for the treatment of any disease or condition"; Epidiolex approved)

claims.claim: Many processors use food-grade ethanol, evaporated off; ethanol and naphtha are flammable
claims.fix: Naphtha dropped with the WebMD citation; now: ethanol is a common choice; extraction solvents like ethanol are flammable.

claims.claim: Swallowed THC passes through the liver first, so it takes longer to kick in than inhaled cannabis and lasts longer
